Are the higher-order rules real? Bootstrap and permutation inference for HONs

honets

2026-08-25

The analytic question

A higher-order network promotes a context to a rule — after Specify → Command, the next action follows a different distribution than after Command alone — whenever a divergence criterion is met in the sample (Xu, Wickramarathne & Chawla 2016). The criterion is a point decision on one dataset. Two questions have to be answered before such rules are reported as findings:

  1. Stability. Would the same rules be extracted from another sample of the same process? bootstrap_hon() resamples sequences with replacement and reports, for every rule, the fraction of replicates that re-extract it (support) and a percentile confidence interval for its conditional probability.
  2. Difference. Do two cohorts follow different rules? compare_hon() tests every pooled rule edge with a permutation null and aggregates a global test, with Benjamini–Hochberg control over the per-edge multiplicity.

Both verbs precompute per-sequence counts once and rebuild every replicate from reweighted counts, so their cost does not grow with sequence length re-scans, and their results are identical in serial and parallel runs under the same seed.

The data are human_long, bundled with honets: 10,796 coded human turns from 429 human–AI pair-programming sessions; each session’s ordered codes form one categorical sequence.

library(honets)

Which rules survive resampling?

Rules are extracted up to order 3, requiring each transition to occur at least 5 times, and every rule is re-examined in 500 bootstrap resamples of the sessions.

bs <- bootstrap_hon(human_long, action = "code", actor = "session_id",
                    time = "timestamp", n_boot = 500, max_order = 3,
                    min_freq = 5, seed = 11, parallel = TRUE, n_cores = 2)
bs
## HON bootstrap: 829 rule edges (748 higher-order) from 425 sequences
##   500 replicates, 95% percentile CIs
##   Higher-order rule support: min 0.35, median 1.00, max 1.00
##   Tidy table: as.data.frame(x); higher-order only: as.data.frame(x, order_min = 2)
summary(bs)

The 425 usable sessions yield 829 rule edges: 81 first-order, 451 second-order, 297 third-order. The summary separates the layers sharply. The second-order layer is solid — mean support 0.995, and even its least stable rule is re-extracted in 89.8% of replicates. The third-order layer is mixed: mean support 0.85, minimum 0.35, and its intervals are wide (mean width 0.70 against 0.20 at order 2). The conclusion is directional: the second-order structure of these sessions can be reported as a whole; third-order claims need the per-rule filter below.

as.data.frame(bs, order_min = 2, min_support = 0.9,
              sort_by = "count", top = 10)
##                             from        to order count probability  ci_lower
## 1             Specify -> Command   Specify     2   284   0.3901099 0.3576493
## 2             Command -> Request   Specify     2   231   0.7674419 0.7229390
## 3             Specify -> Command   Request     2   199   0.2733516 0.2412228
## 4             Request -> Specify Interrupt     2   189   0.3258621 0.2776583
## 5  Specify -> Command -> Request   Specify     3   181   0.9679144 0.9073834
## 6             Command -> Command   Command     2   177   0.3881579 0.3365444
## 7             Command -> Specify Interrupt     2   149   0.2769517 0.2384711
## 8  Command -> Request -> Specify Interrupt     3   136   0.6098655 0.5428544
## 9             Specify -> Request   Specify     2   128   0.6597938 0.6034591
## 10            Specify -> Specify   Specify     2   123   0.2662338 0.2316099
##     ci_upper support n_boot_used
## 1  0.4254156   1.000         500
## 2  0.8412833   0.988         500
## 3  0.3088498   1.000         500
## 4  0.3756526   1.000         500
## 5  1.0000000   0.900         500
## 6  0.4357474   1.000         500
## 7  0.3201072   1.000         500
## 8  0.6915423   0.938         500
## 9  0.7556596   0.980         500
## 10 0.2976057   1.000         500

604 of the 748 higher-order rules pass a 0.9 support floor; the table shows the ten most frequent. The strongest patterns are the directive loop seen from different depths: after Command -> Request the next action is Specify with probability 0.77 (CI 0.72–0.84), and the third-order context Specify -> Command -> Request sharpens this to 0.97 (CI 0.91–1.00, support 0.90). History genuinely narrows the prediction — the deeper context nearly determines the next action, and the bootstrap says that narrowing is not a sampling artifact.

plot(bs, top = 15)

The forest plot makes the layering visible: first- and second-order rules carry tight intervals, third-order rules visibly wider ones.

Did the rules change between the early and late period?

The sessions span 2026-02-05 to 2026-03-08. Splitting the events at the median date gives two cohorts of comparable size (a session straddling the cutoff contributes its early turns to the first cohort and its late turns to the second).

early <- subset(human_long, session_date < "2026-02-21")
late  <- subset(human_long, session_date >= "2026-02-21")
cmp <- compare_hon(early, late, action = "code", actor = "session_id",
                   time = "timestamp", n_perm = 500, max_order = 3,
                   min_freq = 5, seed = 12, parallel = TRUE, n_cores = 2,
                   names = c("early", "late"))
cmp
## HON comparison: early (210 sequences) vs late (217 sequences)
##   828 pooled rule edges, 500 permutations
##   Global weighted |diff|: 0.0875, p = 0.001996
##   Significant edges (BH, alpha = 0.05): 0
##   Tidy table: as.data.frame(x); significant only: as.data.frame(x, significant = TRUE)
summary(cmp)

The two results disagree on purpose, and reading them together is the point of the design. The global test is unambiguous: the pooled-count-weighted mean absolute difference is 0.0875, and only 1 of 501 permutations reaches it (p = 0.002) — the rule structure did shift between the periods. Yet not a single one of the 828 edges is individually significant after Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment. The shift is diffuse: many small, consistent differences spread across the rule set, none large enough to survive 828-way multiplicity on its own. The extreme per-edge differences (absolute difference 1.0 at orders 2–3) are contexts observed in only one period with small counts — exactly the edges a permutation null neutralizes.

The decisive report is therefore: the interaction rules changed over time as a whole, and no single rule should be named as the locus of that change. Naming one anyway — picking the largest difference and reporting it despite its adjusted p-value — is the multiple-testing error this verb’s two-level design exists to prevent.

plot(cmp, top = 15)

The difference plot confirms the reading: the largest differences all plot in the not-significant encoding, and no edge separates from the pack.

When to use which

  • bootstrap_hon() — one cohort, and the question is whether the extracted rules and their probabilities are stable enough to report. Filter with as.data.frame(x, order_min = 2, min_support = 0.9) before citing individual higher-order rules; report interval widths, not just point probabilities.
  • compare_hon() — two cohorts, and the question is whether the rule structure differs. Read the global test first; per-edge findings only from the BH-adjusted column. A significant global with no significant edges is a finding, not a failure: the difference is distributed.
  • markov_order_test() — the prior, coarser question: is there any memory beyond order 1 at all, as a single global decision.
  • path_dependence() — a descriptive per-context diagnostic of where memory concentrates, without inference; useful for choosing contexts to examine before the bootstrap.

References

  • Xu, J., Wickramarathne, T. L., & Chawla, N. V. (2016). Representing higher-order dependencies in networks. Science Advances, 2(5), e1600028.
  • Efron, B., & Tibshirani, R. J. (1993). An Introduction to the Bootstrap. Chapman & Hall.
  • Good, P. (2005). Permutation, Parametric and Bootstrap Tests of Hypotheses (3rd ed.). Springer.
  • Benjamini, Y., & Hochberg, Y. (1995). Controlling the false discovery rate. JRSS B, 57(1), 289–300.
